newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Nobel peace prize puts Australia in awkward position.
newsitem.headline: Nobel peace prize puts Australia in awkward position.

text.p: Australia, virtually alone in recognising Indonesia's rule in East Timor, is faced with a ticklish political problem by the award of the Nobel Peace Prize to a Timorese independence campaigner and a bishop from the former Portugese colony.
The Australian government's reaction on Friday to the news that the award would be shared by Jose Ramos-Horta and Bishop Carlos Belo was muted, and limited to a single sentence.

"We congratulate the Nobel laureates with whom we share the desire for a peaceful East Timor," a spokesman for Australian Foreign Affairs Minister Alexander Downer said. The spokesman declined further comment and Downer himself said nothing.
The Sydney Morning Herald reported on Saturday that senior foreign affairs officials were saying privately that the Nobel Committee's award for Ramos-Horta was "unhelpful".
"I guess Downer will probably duck for cover a bit and not comment, or say very little," one official was quoted as saying.

Andrew MacNaughtan, of the Australian East Timor Association, told the Daily Telegraph newspaper the awards would be an embarrassment to successive Australian governments which, he said, had been inactive on the issue of East Timor.

"This is an 'up-yours' to Gareth Evans, Gough Whitlam, Malcolm Fraser, (Bob) Hawke, (Paul) Keating and (John) Howard", he said, naming Australia's current and previous four prime ministers as well as former Labor foreign minister Evans.
But Harold Crouch, senior fellow in Pacific and Asian studies at Australian National University in Canberra, said he believed the government had responded correctly to the awards.
"It's slightly awkward, I suppose, for the Australian government, but it's not a major challenge," he told Reuters.

Ramos-Horta, who lectures in diplomacy at Sydney's University of New South Wales, said successive Australian governments had not done enough to resolve the situation in East Timor, which is only 500 km (310 miles) north of Australia.
"Australia has been doing next to nothing over the years," said Ramos-Horta, who is among several thousand East Timorese refugees in Australia.
"It has been generous in receiving refugees here and it has raised the issue with the Indonesian government, but it has not done enough to address the root cause of the problem," he said.
"It should be working with the United States and President Clinton, with European leaders, for a joint effort with Indonesia to have Indonesia out of East Timor," he said.
However, he said the Howard government, elected in March, appeared to be more sensitive to the problem than the Keating government, which claimed a special relationship with Indonesia.
"I believe that... the current government now is much more sensitive to the Timor issue, much more sensitive to what is happening in Indonesia," he said.
"I can understand Australia's relationship with Indonesia - Australia cannot choose its neighbours... ," he said.
Ramos-Horta said he planned to meet Downer on October 26, an appointment set up before the Peace Prize was awarded.
The Australian government's handling of its affairs with Indonesia, the country's fastest growing overseas market, is one of its most sensitive foreign policy issues.

Prime Minister Howard was criticised by human rights groups for not highlighting the East Timor issue during a trip to Indonesia in September, emphasising instead the burgeoning economic relationship between the countries.

Relations between Australia and Indonesia went through one of their occasional rough patches late last year when there were violent public protests over the appointment of Lt-Gen Herman Mantiri as Indonesia's ambassador to Australia.
Mantiri had described the 1991 massacre of civilians in East Timor by Indonesian troops as "quite proper."

Earlier this year, Australia's nominee for ambassador to Indonesia was withdrawn after Jakarta protested against the diplomat's one-time criticism of the business interests of President Suharto. Both diplomatic posts have now been filled.
Australia and Indonesia signed a controversial treaty in 1989 to share access to potentially rich oil and gas reserves in the Timor Gap between Australia and the island of Timor.
